newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Low Australian inflation leaves opening for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Low Australian inflation leaves opening for rate cut.

text.p: A fall in Australia's inflation rate to its lowest level in four years has left the door open for a cut in interest rates, but the prevailing view amongst analysts is that rates will remain on hold through 1997.
Official data released on Wednesday showed the consumer price index (CPI) rose just 0.2 percent in the March quarter for an annual inflation rate of 1.3 percent.
This was the lowest level since March 1993, a period which has also seen uninterrupted economic growth.

The underlying inflation rate, a narrower and less volatile measure of the CPI and the rate on which the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) focuses, rose 0.4 percent in the quarter, to be up 2.1 percent over the year.
The RBA aims to keep the underlying rate to an average of between two and three percent over a number of years.

The inflation data came one day after a better than expected outcome to the union movement's "living wage" claim, which had sought an annual A$20 (US$15) a week pay rise over the next three years and an 8.75 percent rise in award rates, which the RBA had warned would threaten low inflation.
Instead lower-paid workers received a A$10 a week pay rise.
"The good inflation result leaves the door open for a further rate cut," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.
However, not many analysts believed rates would be cut.

"It remains the case that the economic outlook for the remainder of 1997 will be one of more low inflation outcomes, but with more signs of accelerating growth," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
When combined with the lift in U.S. rates by the Federal Reserve in March, there was less likelihood of further local rate cuts to follow the three in late 1996, analysts said.
"Talk of a further rate cut is wishful thinking," Axiom Funds Management senior economist Matthew Drennan said.
"The main reason I can't see it is because the banks are already getting that turnaround in the housing sector and that's just a key employment driver," Drennan said.
While that was the majority view, the case for a rate cut has gathered some momentum since mid-February when the RBA said interest rates were on hold.

Since then, some strength in employment data over late 1996 and early 1997 has been revised away, and employment growth has been negative in February and March. Other indicators have also shown some softness after a robust start to 1997.
The stalling of the unemployment rate at around 8.5 percent was a key factor behind the RBA's decision to cut rates last July and was also an influence on the subsequent cuts.
Since the first cut was delivered in July the unemployment rate has not fallen below 8.5 percent and it is a factor that some analysts feel the market has not fully appreciated.

"I suspect the market might be underweighting the level of frustration that might be out there with the slowness of unemployment to improve," Deustche Morgan Grenfell senior economist Bruce Hockman said.
With little threat to low inflation seen in the next year or so, those who saw the need for a rate cut said the RBA could afford to let the economy run a little faster to create jobs.

"The risk for the economy isn't that inflation is going to start picking up, it's that the unemployment rate isn't going to start clicking down," Bankers Trust Australia interest rate strategist Rory Robertson said.
